title: ‘CM Vijay’ WhatsApp call promises Rs 11 lakh aid, Bengaluru man loses Rs 1 lakh

reading.body:
This is an impersonation carried out with synthetic media, not a model making a mistake on its own. A caller used an AI deepfake to present himself, in voice and appearance, as a sitting Chief Minister, and the fraud was built on that false identity. The AI was the instrument of the deception rather than a system that failed at a task it was deployed to do.

The point of failure was the video call itself, a real-time channel on a consumer messaging app where nothing in the pipeline verified who was actually on the other end. The victim had no independent way to confirm the caller's identity, and the payment demands that followed, for exchange charges, a PIN unlock and a fine, were accepted on the strength of the impersonation alone. Catching it would have required authentication of the caller through a channel separate from the call, or detection of the synthetic media at the platform level before it reached the recipient.

What is not established is who made the deepfake or why, and the registration of a case under the Information Technology Act is not a finding against anyone. The account of the call comes from the complainant and a single outlet's reporting, so the technical nature of the impersonation rests on that account rather than on an independent examination.

reports.title: ‘CM Vijay’ WhatsApp call promises Rs 11 lakh aid, Bengaluru man loses Rs 1 lakh

summary:
A 29 year old security guard in Bengaluru, Ratikanta Giri, from Odisha, received a WhatsApp video call on Sept 9 from a number. The caller used an AI deepfake to look and sound like Tamil Nadu Chief Minister Vijay and offered Rs 11 lakh in financial aid. A fake manager then said Rs 5 lakh was allotted and asked for processing payments. This is first such case reported in city.

Giri paid Rs 5,000 as exchange charges, Rs 18,000 to unlock a PIN, over Rs 50,000 as a fake CBI fine, and more, losing over Rs 1.04 lakh. When fraudsters demanded another Rs 50,000, he refused and realized he was duped. He contacted cybercrime helpline 1930 and Byappanahalli police. A case was registered under the Information Technology Act. Police urged people not to trust such calls or make payments based on them.
